Geometrical Reasoning in the History of Astronomy

Fundamentals: Models, Propositions, Steps, Rules, and What the Figure Supplies

Author
Affiliations

Gerd Graßhoff

Humboldt-Universität zu Berlin

Deutsches Museum

Published

November 10, 2026

Abstract

Astronomical texts from Ptolemy to Euler argue geometrically about models: a figure, a few sentences, and inferences marked by little more than “therefore”. This paper gathers what is needed to reconstruct such arguments and to check them. It distinguishes what an argument is about (a model, as pure geometry; values for its parameters; a state) from what it says (propositions) and what it does (operations: to suppose, to construct, to derive, to distinguish cases, to compute, to conclude). It says what licenses a step: an instance of a named proposition, an equality by a Common Notion, a fact read off a construction, a calculation, an expansion in a small ratio. It treats what a figure supplies without saying so — that points are distinct, lie on one side of a line, form a triangle — and what follows when the figure degenerates: cases. It treats hypotheses, how to find out whether an argument needs them, and how to detect one used tacitly; equivalence and identity of models; exact and approximate steps; quantities computed from a model and parameters determined from observations. It fixes a vocabulary for soundness, gives a format in which a reconstructed argument can be read at three depths, a procedure in six steps, and a table of rules with Euclid’s wording and its place. Every notion is shown on one of three cases: Ptolemy’s solar model in Swerdlow’s exposition, Kepler on the equant, and Euler on the tides.

Keywords

history of astronomy, geometrical reasoning, argument reconstruction, Euclid, models, justification

1 What is to be reconstructed

Kepler, arguing against the equant in the Astronomia nova, writes: “DCE exterior aequet CBE, CEB interiores : ergo parte CEB ablata, residuus CBE vel DBE minor erit quam DCE” (Kepler, n.d.). One sentence, one “ergo”. Behind it stand a figure with six letters, a proposition of Euclid about exterior angles, a Common Notion about wholes and parts, and the observation that C and D lie on one ray from B. None of the three is named. A reader of the time supplied them. A reader today who wants to know what Kepler’s argument establishes has to supply them explicitly, and then has something that can be examined: does the proposition apply? In every position of the planet? Does the argument use everything it assumes?

To reconstruct a geometrical argument is to answer three questions in order: what is it about, what does it say, and by what right does it move from one statement to the next. This paper sets out the notions needed for each and the way they are checked. The notions are implemented in the language astra/1 (Graßhoff 2026a); three reconstructions made with them are published separately (Graßhoff 2026d, 2026c, 2026b). Here they are gathered.

2 What an argument is about

2.1 Model, values, state

An astronomical argument is about a model. Four things are easily taken for one (Figure 1).

The model is the pure geometry: points, lines and circles, each constructed from what precedes it; lengths and angles as parameters, which are symbols with a unit and an admissible range; and one or more kinematic variables, the quantities whose change is the motion. The model has no values. What is true of it is true for every admissible value of its parameters and every value of its variables.

A parametrisation gives the parameters values, each with the place where it stands in a source, and says whose values they are. One model has many: Ptolemy’s solar model with Ptolemy’s values, with al-Battānī’s, and with the exaggerated eccentricity of a printed figure.

A state is a value of the kinematic variable. A model under a parametrisation in a state is a configuration: everything has a place. A figure shows one configuration.

A geometrical argument is about the model, not about a configuration. This is why it has to be checked over the parameter space and the states, and why a figure, which is one configuration, can mislead.

2.2 Three roles

Every text about a model involves three parties that must not be confused: whose model it is (attributed), the text whose use of the model is analysed (witness), and who wrote the description (author). Ptolemy’s solar model, read in Swerdlow’s exposition and described by a third person, has three different names in these three places. An exposition is not an authorship.

2.3 Several models at once

Many arguments are about two models: that they are equivalent, that one can replace the other. The scene of such an argument is a superposition: the models in one plane, with their inputs identified — one observer, one direction of the apsidal line, one mean motion. A superposition adds no geometry and asserts nothing across its members. That two constructed points of different members coincide is a proposition, and propositions are argued.

3 What an argument says

An argument consists of propositions. Only propositions are true or false. A sentence of the text renders a proposition; a figure renders none.

A proposition is true of the model: in every configuration. That is a strong reading, and it is the one the texts intend when they argue from a figure in general position. Where an author means one position — Kepler’s “et sit jam DCE rectus” — the argument says so, by a supposition (Section 4).

A proposition is checked by turning it into a number that is zero when it holds, its residual, and evaluating that number in many configurations: sampled points of the parameter space, each parameter in its admissible range, and the kinematic variable through a revolution. This is evidence, not proof (Section 11).

4 What an argument does

An argument is a sequence of operations on propositions (Table 2).

A premise of a step is one of four things: a given; an earlier step; the construction of an object (“C lies on the deferent” is read off how C was constructed); or the condition of the case or supposition under which the step stands.

Sub-arguments give an argument its shape. The claim stands first, its steps below, indented. The inside of a sub-argument is local: a step outside may cite the sub-argument, not a step inside it. This is what makes an overview possible. At the coarsest depth an argument is its top-level sub-arguments and its conclusion (Figure 2).

5 What licenses a step

A step is a proposition together with a claim about it: that it follows from these premises by this rule. The proposition may be true and the claim false. Five kinds of licence occur (Table 3).

A rule is stated as a schema: variables for points, hypotheses, conclusions, and conditions on the configuration (Section 6). For I.33 the schema is: from parallel(line(A, B), line(C, D)) and equal(distance(A, B), distance(C, D)) to parallel(line(A, C), line(B, D)) and equal(distance(A, C), distance(B, D)). The match respects the symmetries of the propositions: parallel and equal are symmetric, a line and a distance do not depend on the order of their points, an angle is unsigned.

The grades are not equally strong, and the display shows which a step has. An instance of a named proposition is the strongest: the step can be handed to anyone with a copy of Euclid. “Read off the construction” says that nothing but the definitions is used; its test is that the proposition holds when all hypotheses are lifted. “Calculation” is the weakest: the program confirms the result and does not replay the reckoning.

Table 4 is the table of rules in use. A proposition of Euclid enters it only after its wording has been compared with a page of Heath’s translation (Euclid 1908).

6 What the figure supplies

Euclid’s propositions take things from the figure that their enunciations do not state. I.33 speaks of “equal and parallel straight lines” joined “at the extremities which are in the same directions”: the two lines must point the same way, and the four points must not lie on one line. I.32 speaks of a triangle. I.28 needs the two points on the same side of the transversal. In a schema these are configuration conditions:

A figure supplies them silently, for the position it shows. An argument about a model needs them in every position. So they are evaluated in every sampled configuration, and a state in which one fails is a degenerate state of the step: there the rule does not apply.

Degenerate states are where figures mislead. The parallelogram OESC by which the two forms of Ptolemy’s solar model are shown equivalent exists in every position of the sun but two. At the apogee and at the perigee the four points lie on one line (Figure 3). The conclusion is true there as well, and the argument does not reach it.

The figure of this argument in motion, drawn from the model: the mean anomaly runs through a revolution, and the steps of the construction can be shown one after the other.

The remedy is a distinction of cases. A case has a condition; its steps are checked only in the configurations that satisfy it; the cases must together cover every configuration; and each must reach the claim. A degenerate state that is not covered by a case is reported. An argument with cases is longer than its figure suggests, and that is a finding about the argument.

7 Hypotheses

A hypothesis is something the argument assumes of the parameters: that the epicycle has the radius of the eccentricity; that the equant lies as far above the centre as the eye lies below. It is not part of the model. Keeping it out of the model makes three questions answerable.

Is it needed? The test repeats the check with the hypothesis lifted: the parameter it fixed is sampled freely. A proposition that then fails needs the hypothesis. For the equivalence of the two solar models, both hypotheses on the radii are needed. For Kepler’s argument that the equant makes the planet move unequally about the centre of its circle, the hypothesis that the eccentricity is bisected is not needed: the conclusion holds wherever the equant point lies above the centre (Figure 4).

Is it cited? A step that needs a hypothesis which is not cited on the way to it rests on a tacit premise. The argument may be true throughout and still not say what it uses.

Is anything assumed that is never used? A hypothesis that no step needs is noted. It may belong to the model as the author knows it and play no part in this argument.

A supposition differs from a hypothesis. A hypothesis restricts the parameters; a supposition restricts the states. Kepler’s right angle is a supposition. Where a supposition stands matters: placed late, it shows how much of the argument holds without it. In Figure 4 the two inequalities (1 and 4) hold in every position; only the comparison of two arcs passed in equal times (6) needs the right angle.

8 Equivalence and identity

Two texts describe the same model when they are the same geometry up to the names of things. Two models are equivalent when, under stated hypotheses, they agree in what is compared. The comparison has to be named:

  • equivalent in position: the bodies of the two models are at one point in every state;
  • equivalent in direction: they are seen from the observer in one direction; the distances may differ.

The eccentric and the epicyclic form of the solar model are equivalent in position when R′ = R and r = e, and in direction when only R′/r = R/e. They are never the same model: in one the sun moves uniformly on a circle, in the other its motion is compounded of two. An equivalence is the conclusion of an argument in the superposition of the two models. It is never a premise, and a diagram that draws two bodies as one point has assumed what is to be shown.

9 Exact and approximate

From the seventeenth century on, arguments end in approximations. Euler obtains the force that raises the tides exactly and then expands it in the ratio of the earth’s size to the distance of the moon. A step of this kind is the proposition approximately(a, b, small: ρ / a, order: n). It is checked by making the ratio small — a hundredth, a thousandth, a ten-thousandth — and requiring the relative difference of the two sides to fall like the n-th power of the ratio.

The order is part of the proposition, and it can decide a textual question. In the second-order term of one of Euler’s components the Opera omnia print 4xx + yy, an editorial emendation; the first edition and the manuscript have 4xx − yy. Stated to second order, the original reading holds and the emended one does not (Graßhoff 2026d).

10 Quantities

Some assertions of a text are not about the model but about a model with values.

To compute is to evaluate a quantity of the model under a parametrisation: the largest equation of centre under Ptolemy’s values is 2;23°. The result is compared with the number the text gives, at the precision in which that number is written.

To determine is the inverse: parameters are found from observations through the model. Ptolemy finds the eccentricity and the apogee of the sun from the lengths of two seasons. The model is inverted numerically for the unknown parameters, and it is reported whether the solution is the only one. This can separate what follows from the data from what follows from the author’s rounding: Ptolemy’s two parameters follow from his rounded arcs of mean motion, not from the day counts with exact arithmetic (Graßhoff 2026b).

11 Soundness: a vocabulary

The words matter, and they are used here as follows.

  • True and false are said of propositions. A step is true when its proposition is.
  • Justified is said of a step: its rule licenses it. The criterion of a good argument is justification. The program does not “verify” Kepler; it reports which steps are justified and how.
  • An argument is sound when every proposition in it is true and every step is justified. An argument with a false premise is unsound; its conclusion is not thereby false.
  • An argument is conclusive when it is sound and the conclusion rests only on what is cited.
  • Evidence is not proof. The checks evaluate propositions in sampled configurations and match rules as schemas. They can show that a step is false, that it is not an instance of its rule, or that it needs a hypothesis. They cannot prove a proposition for all configurations.

Four levels follow, each presupposing the one before: grounded (every premise resolves), true, justified, conclusive.

12 The display

A reconstructed argument is read by people. The format astra-argument/1 fixes a reading order and three depths.

The order: the model (every object with its construction and its astronomical meaning); what is given; the argument; the conclusion; what the checks say.

The argument is a numbered outline. Sub-arguments and cases are indented. A row has four places: the number, the claim as a sentence, the rule at the right margin, and a mark for the kind of licence (✓ an instance of the rule, ◦ read off the construction, ≈ calculation or expansion, ? true but not justified, ✗ false). Below the claim stand the proposition in the notation of the figure (“OE ∥ CS”) and the premises as references to other rows.

The three depths: overview shows the top-level sub-arguments and the conclusion; steps shows every step with its claim, notation, premises and rule; full adds the formal proposition, the binding of the rule’s variables, what the rule takes from the figure, the degenerate states, and the wording of the proposition with its place in Heath.

The same document is rendered three ways: as the interactive element <astra-argument>, in which every block opens and closes and a selected step is shown in the figure; as the printed outline of Figure 2 and Figure 4; and as plain text.

13 A procedure

  1. Fix the passage. An edition with addressable paragraphs; the quotations checked against the transcription.
  2. Write the model. Every object of the figure with a construction and a meaning; lengths and angles as symbols; what varies; whose model it is.
  3. Separate hypotheses from geometry. What the author assumes of the lengths is a hypothesis.
  4. Write the steps. One proposition per step, in the author’s order, with the author’s words as the gloss; for every “therefore” the premises and the rule. Suppositions where the author fixes a position, placed where they are first needed. Sub-arguments where a paragraph proves one thing.
  5. Run the checks. Grounded, true, justified, conclusive.
  6. Read the report as a finding about the text. Which steps are instances of propositions; which are read off the figure; which hypotheses are needed; which positions are not covered; which numbers follow.

Listing 1 and Listing 2 show the result for Kepler’s argument.

14 What is missing

The table of rules holds what three reconstructions needed. Astronomy needs more, and some of it is not yet within reach.

  • Plane geometry. Further propositions of Books I, III and VI — the angle at the centre and at the circumference (III.20), the angle in a semicircle (III.31), triangles cut by a parallel (VI.2) — enter when a reconstruction needs them and their wording has been compared.
  • Chords. Ptolemy computes with a table of chords. The model can be inverted exactly; Ptolemy’s own steps cannot be followed until the Almagest is available in addressable form.
  • The sphere. Latitude, rising times and eclipses need spherical geometry and the theorem of Menelaus. The present models are planar.
  • Proof. The checks give evidence. A symbolic check of the steps marked “calculation” and “read off the construction” would close the distance to a proof for the cases that are exact.
  • Hypotheses. A hypothesis has to fix a parameter. Inequalities between parameters are expressed by admissible ranges, not as hypotheses.

15 Conclusion

A geometrical argument about an astronomical model can be taken apart into what it is about, what it says and what it does, and each part can be written so that it can be checked. The decisive distinctions are few: the model against its values and its states; a proposition against the claim that it follows; a hypothesis against a supposition; what a proposition says against what it takes from the figure; equivalence against identity; truth against justification. With them, three texts from three centuries yielded findings of the same kind: what the argument uses, how far it reaches, and where the figure does not show what the argument needs.
